utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, I think some protective measures have been ordered in respect of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Pseudonym and face distortion is what he requested, because his family requested him to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do we have any objections from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. Protective measures will be applied. The pseudonym for this witness will be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness D, can you hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I can hear you very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness D. First of all, you are now going to read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me first of all bid good morning to everybody here in the courtroom. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down, Witness D. The registrar is going to show you a piece of paper with your name on it. You're simply going to tell us if the name written on the paper is yours or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness D, for coming here to testify. I hope that you are comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my obligation as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We do take note of that. You are first going to answer questions put to you by Mr. McCloskey, who is representing the Prosecution. Mr. McCloskey, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness D, can you first tell us your date of birth and where you were born, and remember, and I'll remind myself, not to speak too fast.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I was born on the (redacted), in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I grew up in the area around the town of Srebrenica and in the town of Srebrenica as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What kind of education have you had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I'm a machine operator by profession, but I also did some additional training as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Prior to the outbreak of the war, where were you living and who were you living with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Prior to the outbreak of the war, I lived with my wife and my child in our house in the village of Solocusa on the outskirts of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How old is your child now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What was your occupation? What were you doing prior to the outbreak of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were their bauxite mine companies in other towns near Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, there were. There was a bauxite mine that was opened in the municipality of Vlasenica, and it was only in 1982 that such a mine opened in the municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me take you to July 11th of 1995. Can you tell me where you were then and what you did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, 1995, I was in my house because I had been wounded. I had been wounded at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you and your family decide to do something that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: On that day, I decided to go towards Potocari, because I believed that I would be protected there because I was a wounded person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you take your family with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I did. My wife went with me, together with our small child, who was five at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why did you feel a need to go to Potocari? Can you tell us a bit about the events that caused you to go there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I felt the need to leave because there had been so much hatred in Srebrenica during the war, and because of that hatred, it was obvious that people had become fearful. I wanted someone to offer me some kind of protection because I was wounded, and I expected that the Dutch Battalion would be able to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was the Bosnian Serb army nearby on July 11th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, it was. According to what I was able to see, units of the Serbian army were advancing. They may have already entered the town -- I think that they did, actually -- from the direction of Zeleni Jadar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you just stay in your house and let them advance around you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Well, this would have been very difficult. I would have been dead, because everybody who remained ended up dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Where did you go when you got to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: When we got to Potocari, I saw a huge crowd of people there. I didn't have any adequate accommodation at all. I went to a factory hall which was part of the factory intended for inspection of vehicles, and I happened to find a spot in one of the corners of that hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was that known as a bus company or a bus compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, it was. They were in charge of providing certain transport services in Srebrenica. They were carrying out maintenance and technical inspection of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know about what time you arrived in Potocari and went inside the building of the bus compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I couldn't be very precise, but I think, as far as I can remember, that it must have been around noon on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you do that afternoon and evening, and your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: In the afternoon of that day I personally remained in that building. Meanwhile, my wife went to fetch some food for our child in the evening. It should be important to stress that my wife is from Potocari. Their [sic] parents had a house in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was she able to get some supplies from that house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. She went there, took certain things, talked to her father, and that was the last time she saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened, if anything, that first evening in Potocari at the bus compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Nothing particular except that we could hear powerful detonations of shells. I believe the artillery was used to shell the centre of the town and the surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the situation inside the compound; how many people, what their condition was, how they were feeling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: In a nutshell, it was horrible. Very many people in a very tight space. It was crowded. Children were crying. Needless to say, they needed to go to the lavatory. There was little food. They were lying down on the concrete floor. Their mothers somehow tried to manage. They brought hay from nearby meadows and spread that on the floor so that the children wouldn't have to lie on concrete.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you get any sleep that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I did not manage to fall asleep that night, because I was in a sitting position, and I tried to sleep, but I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And on the morning, the next morning of July 12th, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The next morning dawned and these scenes were almost the same, except that panic was mounting among the people there. And later on that morning I saw Serb soldiers in the same hall in which we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what caused the panic to mount that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The mere presence of the Serb soldiers, even though I must point out that those Serb soldiers behaved very decently. I could give you some description of those Serb soldiers. They looked different. They were dressed differently than the military who came from around Srebrenica; that is, they had somewhat better uniforms and their speech reminded me of the way that they speak in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, where were these soldiers when you actually were able to see them and hear them speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: You mean the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: They entered in groups of two or three and they moved amongst the people, seeking their identity documents. They particularly asked for identification documents from men, perhaps to check who those men were, and I guess it was their task, that it must have been a special group of soldiers tasked with checking who was among those civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how many of those soldiers did you actually hear speaking?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Well, I could hear two groups, perhaps. One group talked to me personally and another one was in the immediate vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did they say to you personally?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: They asked to see my ID, and I showed it to them. And they asked me why I was there, and I told them that I had been wounded. They asked me when was I wounded. When I gave them the date, they said, "Fine."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And roughly what time was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It could have been -- well, I saw them sometime in the morning, so it could have been around noon sometime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever make an effort to look outside the bus compound or did you pretty much stay inside the compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Since the door had been removed, there was no door, and the doorway was very broad, very wide, so one could see lots of people outside too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you ever see any Muslim men taken out of the compound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I did not see that that day, but in the office where they conducted technical inspection of vehicles, I noticed that Ibrahim Mustafic and Hamid -- I can't remember his last name -- were missing. They were involved actually in politics. They were in the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened to Ibrahim Mustafic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: They must have taken him away for some kind of interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what eventually happened to Ibrahim Mustafic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: We know today that he is alive, that he was exchanged at Pale, which means that he had been taken to Pale for some interviews, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How long did you stay inside the bus compound on July 12th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Towards the dusk, in late afternoon. From those women and men who wanted to go out, to leave, on that 12th, we heard that men were being separated, and that frightened me, so that naturally I tried to find some safety, to find a safer place where I wouldn't be noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I thought that the buses in front of the building could provide -- could prove a good shelter. Let me explain it. Those were buses which belonged to the Srebrenica Express Depot, but they had been completely broken down. There were no window panes or anything, no wheels or anything. And I happened to be on such a bus next to the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you take your family into that bus next to the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. My wife and my child were also in that bus, and on our way there we found -- we came across my mother, who also wanted to be with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So your mother was in the bus also?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. She joined us as we were moving towards that bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you spend the night of July 12th in that bus with your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. I spent the night with my family in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you ever leave the bus that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No, I did not leave the bus that night, because one could feel -- one could hear -- one heard screams, loud screams, of women, of children; children were crying and screaming. It was beyond description, and I shall never forget that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe it in a little more detail, what it was like that night, what you heard, what you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I could not see anything because I was sitting down in that bus, and all around us and in the immediate vicinity, one could hear loud screams such as, "Let me go," "Don't," "Please let me be," "Leave me alone," women crying, women screaming, asking for help. All this was creating panic, creating an atmosphere of fear. The atmosphere seemed to be boiling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When the morning finally came, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: When the day broke at long last, I decided to start in the same direction as other people; that is, to try to leave that area, because I could see that that was the only solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Prior to you leaving the bus, did your wife go outside the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. My wife wanted to find some water for the child. And as I have said in the beginning, she used to live in Potocari. She knew well every house in Potocari. So she went to a house across the road to fill a bottle with water, that is, about a litre of water. When she came back, she told me that she had seen a lot of blood on the ground floor of that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So then what did you decide to do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Well, naturally I was shaken by that. But I asked my wife not to tell that to my mother, because she was terribly afraid as to what might happen next. I picked up the child, and I headed for the group at the exit where there were two UN APCs parked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What were your intentions at this time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I wanted to get out. I simply could not stand it any longer. And I was thinking, even if I'm separated from them, right, I'm separated, but if I leave, I've left. There was no other way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Well, I found myself in an even bigger crowd of people, because everybody was trying to get out. When I say "people," I mean both women and children, and a few men were still in the same crowd, still. I managed to, after quite a long period of time, that is, after an hour or perhaps even more, I somehow managed to make my way to those APCs, to the exit, and I was carrying my child with me. My wife and my mother were not far from me, but they were somewhat lagging behind in all that throng.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And keep describing what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. I managed to get through, and as I came to the APCs, and I have said that they were to the left and to the right-hand side of the road, and in front of those APCs were UN soldiers, their hands tied together into two lines so as to prevent uncontrolled passage; that is, one had to -- only several people could pass through at a time, not the whole crowd together. I managed to get through. Then I saw Serb soldiers who had already reached the buses had moved away for a moment, and I think that somebody must have called them and they just moved away for a moment, and that proved to be a correct assumption later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when these Serb soldiers left for a moment, what did you and your family do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I boarded a bus, and so did my family, my wife and my mother, and I was carrying the child, as I said. So I got on the bus and immediately ran next to the -- next to the rear door of the bus. I just made two or three steps and I sat down on the floor of the bus. My wife followed suit, and my mother, and I should say about ten women or so with children also got on the bus. So I was quite covered by them as I was sitting on the floor. After that, I heard some male voices, rather, Serb soldiers asking whether there were any men on the bus. Nobody answered. None of those women said anything, and they did not insist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So were you trying to hide from the Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, as a matter of fact. And I did hide from those Serb soldiers because the bodies of those children and women hid me. After that, more people crowded on to the bus, women and children, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why did you feel a need to hide from the Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It is quite clear why I felt such need. Because they were separating all men and, naturally, I was afraid that they might separate me too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you afraid something might happen to you after you were separated or if you were separated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Naturally, because of this major hatred, as I said in the beginning. I knew that this major hatred had developed amongst the Serbs, and because of that hatred, anything could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So after you got on the bus and other people got on the bus, what was the next thing that occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The bus was overcrowded by that time, and the driver tried to shut the doors several times. It was very difficult, because there were just too many people. But he finally managed to do that, and the bus headed for Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe that trip? What you know of it anyway.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. What I could hear on the bus, that is, women in the bus were commenting where the bus was going, and they said, "Now we're in Bratunac." "Now we're here." "Now we're there." So they were saying that all the time until the bus stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell, from what they were saying, what direction the bus was going in besides Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. The bus started in towards Bratunac and then went on towards Vlasenica, through Glogova, Kravica, Konjevic Polje, Nova Kasaba, Milici, on to Vlasenica, Tisca, Luke, and that was the last stop where all the buses stopped on a large ground, in a large concrete area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you ever look out of the bus at any time during this trip?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. In Kravica, we heard loud screams and crying, shrieks of women and children. I could not but look as to what was going on, so I stood up from where I was sitting, looked to the left and right of the windows of the bus and I saw men, some who were lying down in the meadow, and they did not seem to be moving, and others who had been captured, with their arms and hands up behind their -- at the neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell about how many men you saw captured with their hands and arms around their neck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I think it must have been a group of about 50 or slightly more people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell who these people were, whether they were Serbs or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: They were Muslims. I can positively claim that because they were wearing civilian clothes, and they looked horrified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were there any soldiers anywhere near them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. Near them were several Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were those soldiers armed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The Serb soldiers, yes, they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: After that, on the trip towards Luke, did anything else significant occur that you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: On our way to Luke, the bus was stopped several times, and they also thought to check whether there were any men, but the driver behaved decently and kept telling them that he was taking only women and children. At some point, they wanted to check that. They asked him to open both the front and the rear door. He had to open them, of course, but they did not spot me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any other men on the bus you were on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: In that bus I did see a man but of a very advanced age. He must have been 70 at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you just saw one other man or more?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Only one in that bus. I did not see any other man on the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. What happened when the bus stopped at Luke?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: When the bus reached its destination, that is, that platform, I heard the driver, who said to women and children, "You have to get off here and proceed on foot because your folk are nearby and you will reach them in no time."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what did you do and your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I got off the bus too with my child in my arms. My wife had her backpack on her back, and she was supporting my mother because she was old and very frail. So she was looking after my mother, and I was taking care of my child and had it in my arms. My child was five years old. After we had got off the bus and had made just a few steps, I noticed several Serb soldiers. One of those Serb soldiers pulled me by the shoulder and said, "Give the child to your wife and you come with us." I had to do that. So I gave the child to my wife. I tried to turn once again, because I knew that was the last time I would see my child. As a matter of fact, I was about to say something. I wanted to say anything, but then I couldn't. At that moment, the Serb soldier pushed me with his rifle and said, "Move on." Then he turned to a man who was sitting on a slight elevation by the road and who was wearing camouflage trousers and a sweater, and he said, "Major, what do we do with him?" And that man indicated with his hand, and he was pointing towards the rear, towards backward.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I started in front of that Serb soldier. He was a few steps behind me. All of a sudden, he said, "I seem to know you. Did you work for (redacted) perhaps?" And I said, "Yes, I did." So he said, "Do you know me?" I answered, "Perhaps from sight but not really." Then he said that he had worked as a surveyor and that I surely remembered him, because he, as he said, used to come to our company quite often because he was surveying that mine. I mean, he did his surveyor's job and often came to the mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you in fact recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: His face was familiar, but I didn't know his name. And we continued along that road and then we turned left. And there I noticed a structure. It was the Luke school. And he brought me right -- we fetched up right up in front of the house, of the school, because I noticed and I recognised a young fellow from Srebrenica, whose hands were tied behind his back, and that fellow's name was Abdul Kadir. As a matter of fact, he was a medical -- a lab technician, and he used to work for the war hospital in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me take you back a little bit. When you were speaking to this person that identified himself as a surveyor, and he was speaking to you, do you understand the various accents of the regions? I know you described earlier some accents of Potocari. Do you understand, do you know the accents of the regions of Eastern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I am familiar with the dialects of the area. He spoke normally, the way we do, I mean we Bosnians who lived in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was the direction that the person that he referred to as "the Major," was the direction the Major pointed in, was that the direction you went in to the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We continued in the direction which was indicated by that man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know about what time you arrived at the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Well, my assumption is that it may have been sometime around 10.00 a.m., or perhaps a little later than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this time I'd like to show the witness a few exhibits. If we could start with Exhibit 10/1. And that's a panorama. And if I could ask a little help with the ELMO on that so he can ...

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: On this photograph one can see the school building. We were brought to the front of that school. If you want me to, I can show you also the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you maybe point out on the road anything that you recognise, and tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I can. So we came -- we were going towards this place here [indicates]. We were moving in this direction. We went off the road here [indicates] and found ourselves in this part here [indicates], in front of the school building. So this is where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I have to interrupt for one second. Indicating, for the record, it appeared he started at the end of the road where it goes out of view and brought the pointer back towards the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell from this photograph, can you see the general area where you first were stopped and separated from your family?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: As far as I can see, in the back you can perhaps see one structure in the distance. It's a house. And as far as I could observe, at the time there was indeed a house next to the road, which had some business premises as well. So the house was not far from here, where I'm indicating [indicates]. We continued along the road and then turned off and went to the area in front of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And for the record, he indicated sort of the end of the road as it goes out of our view is the area where he started, and then he came back and turned towards the -- what is the left side of the house on the photograph. Could we show the witness Exhibit 10/2.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. Here as well one can see the school building. There is a little path here leading behind the school. It is going to be mentioned later on in one of the testimonies. This is where the truck left with prisoners [indicates]. You can see this area here, this clearing in front of the school, and we were standing on this far side of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Again, excuse me, Witness D. I just for the record need to indicate that you first pointed to what appears to be tyre tracks on the left side of the school, and then you came around in the front of the school and where some white vehicles are parked. Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No. Maybe we don't understand each other very well. I said that this spot would be mentioned later on. At that time we were still standing on that side. I'm just saying that I can see this particular path, which will become important later on. But for a while we were standing, or rather sitting, at the far end of the school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you point where you were standing or sitting when you first got to the school, with the pointer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: You can't see the exact spot here, but it was in the area behind the school. The area cannot be seen on this photograph. Maybe you will have a more clear picture later on. And later on we will see that there is a tree here [indicates]. And I hope I'll be able to indicate it on a better photograph later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. For the record, he was pointing to the area just in front of the white trucks. And if we could go to the next exhibit, 10/3.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. This is where you can see it clearly. This is what I was talking about. You can see the part of the school that I mentioned. You can see the stairs, which I will also mention later on. This is the tree I was referring to and underneath which we were sitting at the time. I know it very well. Here you can see the access road leading from the asphalt road [indicates]. It was actually a small path which could not be used by trucks or other vehicles. So we came from that direction over there and we found a man sitting here, whose hands were tied, and me and Abdul Kadir were sitting here next to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And for the record, the area of access of the building appeared to be an area near bush. In the right-hand corner of the photo it looks like there's a slight worn area there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I guess you could call it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can we see the next exhibit, which is 10/4.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: On this particular photograph we can see the classroom where we were brought in. Later on I will tell you more about that. I will explain how it happened. The classrooms were all the same. We were brought to one of the classrooms first and then to another one. There was no furniture at the time in any of the classrooms, so these pictures must have been taken later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's all we need from the exhibits for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what happened, as you remember it, during the course of the day while you were sitting in this area?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We may have a little glitch. Let me try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness D, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It's only now that I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell the Court what you did during the course of the day by the side of this building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Immediately after I had arrived, after I was brought in by this Serbian soldier that I mentioned, my hands were tied by some shoelaces, or boot laces, by other soldiers, and I was ordered to sit down next to this man, this young man, whom I have already mentioned, whose name I have mentioned. So I was sitting in the grass in front of the building and I could observe other people being brought in. As the time went by, the number of people constantly increased. My back was turned towards the road, but I could still hear the sound of trucks and buses coming and leaving. So throughout that day I sat on that meadow in the grass. There were other people coming in and they were also sitting in our vicinity. Not everybody was tied up. Mostly young men were being tied up. Elderly people were not tied up. Later you will probably read in one of the statements that everybody had been tied with a wire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you: Were you tied up with your hands in front or in the back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: My hands were tied up in the back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about the person you've identified as Abdul -- I forgot the last part of his name -- as Abdul.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Abdul Kadir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were his hands tied also?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, his hands were tied as well. They were also tied in the back, like my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And by the end of the day, how many people had been brought to the group, total?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: All together there were 22 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what were the age ranges, roughly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There were younger men as well, up to 20 years of age, but there were also some elderly people, people over 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What do you think was the youngest person that was in your group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I think that the youngest person was Abdul Kadir, actually, and I believe that he was 19 or 20, or perhaps even younger than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you describe what occurred in front of you besides all these men being brought to your location? What were you able to see from your position here that happened that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you about that. I was simply sitting there. I had a lot of time. I was able to observe Serb soldiers coming and leaving the area. They were probably leaving for other assignments, other tasks. Some were threatening us, whereas others behaved in a normal way. I saw a soldier who was only answering the telephone. It was a kind of military telephone that had been set up on the stairway that I have indicated on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What made you think it was a military telephone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I was very familiar with that kind of telephone. It was a field telephone which we used in the Yugoslav People's Army. So I knew very well this particular type of telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able to hear any of the statements or conversations that the Serb soldiers on the phone were making?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I could hear only the words spoken by this soldier whom they referred to as Zeljko. Zeljko was one of those who behaved decently. While he was talking on the telephone, he would simply say, "Yes, sir. Yes, I'll do that. I will tell them that. Everything is okay," something to that effect. Those were his answers to the telephone calls.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you recognise any of the Serb soldiers that were at this location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I did. The first person I recognised was the man who told me his name was Stanimir himself, but he also mention that in a conversation with Abdul Kadir. He actually approached us and he talked to Abdul Kadir more. At one point he said, do you know that you and your father are friends?" And Abdul Kadir replied that, yes, he remembered him a little. At that point the man told him that his name was Stanimir, that he lived in Vlasenica, that he had a flat there and a car, and I remember noticing that he had arrived in a red car, Lada type. I also recognised Savo Ristanovic. He was one of the soldiers whose hair was very fair, blonde. At one point he approached two prisoners, that is, the people who had been brought from the buses. He came near to them and they told him they had recognised him, and they addressed him as a neighbour. This man said, "How are you, neighbour?" But the man got very angry. He said, "Why are you asking me how I am? First of all, you should tell me who set my grandfather's house on fire." But these two, one of them must have said, "We do not know." Their names were Fuad and Alija, and I knew them. They had been wounded, these two individuals. Then he told them, "You will probably learn who that was who had set my grandfather's house on fire." There were lots of Serb soldiers coming in, leaving the area. Many of them threatened us, but they did not beat us. We were not beaten until we got into the school building. They were very menacing. They were cursing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Are you sure it was Savo Ristanovic that you saw or was there some confusion on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Savo Ristanovic, I knew his family name. I know that his family name is Ristanovic, but later on, after I had reached the free territory and in some discussions with my friends, their wives told me or, rather, confirmed his identity. Those women had also been there. They had been brought in buses. At that moment, I couldn't remember his Christian name, but they told him that his name was Savo. Somebody else was also asking about his grandfather's house and some other problems that apparently had been happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was there a Momcilo Ristanovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Momcilo Ristanovic was also a cousin of his. They looked alike very much. So when I talked to my colleagues, first of all I thought that it had been Momcilo Ristanovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Ristanic"], but they corrected me and they told me that they knew him very well, and they told me that it had been Savo Ristanovic, but the two are cousins.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me get back to Stanimir for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. McCloskey, but I heard other French or English interpreters speak about a Ristanovic, but the transcript says "Ristanic." Is there any difference between the two? You could perhaps repeat whether we are speaking about a man by the name of Ristanovic or Ristanic. The witness has said "Ristanovic." This is what I've been told just now by the interpreter, but I can still see on the transcript "Ristanic." Could it be investigated please, and could you repeat the question to the witness, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did Stanimir, the person you've identified as Stanomir, talk to you about anything or anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Stanimir, that is the Serb soldier, was talking to Abdul Kadir for a while, and during that time I was sitting next to Abdul Kadir. At one point he turned to me and he asked me where I had worked before. So I told him that I had worked in (redacted) (redacted) Srebrenica. Then he told me, "So you probably know (redacted), one of our guys who also used to work in the (redacted) company in Srebrenica," and I told him that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, know this person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. I knew him quite well. Let me please -- are you referring to Stanimir or (redacted) (redacted) here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good question. (redacted), please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I knew (redacted) very well. He was a colleague of mine. We used to work together, because for a while we were in the same department. We were very good colleagues and we were friends as well, and we used to work together for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, again I'm sorry for interrupting you, but I can see that the transcript is somehow disappearing. My question concerned two family names, "Ristanic" and "Ristanovic." That is what I wanted to know exactly, but I cannot see this on the transcript. I think that we are talking about two different names, and the French interpreter has confirmed that the witness said "Ristanovic." My question concerning -- my question, as it appears on the transcript, does not reflect this distinction. I said "Ristanic" and then "Ristanovic." I'm sorry to insist on this, but I would like to know what the name of the person is. Is it "Ristanovic" or "Ristanic"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. I thought the interpreter had cleared that issue up for you. I didn't realise you wanted me to do that, but I can do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is true the interpreters have enlightened me, but this is not reflected on the transcript, and that's why I ask the question again. Be that as it may, I think you could ask the witness whether this was one in the same person and whether the name of the person was "Ristanic" or "Ristanovic." I think these are two different names. At least this is how I hear them. I can tell that there is a difference. I do apologise for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness, can you perhaps clear this up? What was the name of the person that you recognised? What was the last name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. It is important to be very precise here. The man's name was not "Ristanic" but "Ristanovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The record should reflect that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Back to your conversation with Stanimir. You told us that he had mentioned a person named (redacted) and that you had actually known (redacted). Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, it is. He mentioned (redacted), and I asked him if it was possible for me to see (redacted) (redacted), and I inquired as to the way it could be done. But he simply laughed a little, and he said, "Well, he's out in the field today, together with his soldiers, but you will see him in the evening." So we went on talking. He spoke about (redacted) function in the army, and he said that (redacted) was a Commander of a Special Intervention Unit. He also said that he was at Kravica, in the field, and that he had a mission to do there, and he said that I would see him when that task is completed. He said that he would come later on in the evening. And he praised (redacted) a lot. He said he was a very good man, that he had done a lot for the VRS, and he also said that he felt -- that he had been honoured with the task of hoisting up a flag of the Serbian soldiers' unit somewhere in Srebrenica. He seemed to be delighted with (redacted) (redacted). And he also said that (redacted) had been very successful in his sabotage actions. One of them was when they entered Srebrenica, near the tunnel. And then we continued speaking, and he wanted to know what happened when (redacted) men entered the area. And I too praised (redacted), because I didn't want to contradict him. I told him that they had done a lot, their soldiers, that their action had been very successful, but the truth is that in that action, they had killed a number of civilians, including women and children, that there had been a number of houses on fire, and that there was a lot of shooting going on, and that after that they withdrew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What is this tunnel that was referred to by Stanimir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Stanimir mentioned a tunnel which belonged to the lead and zinc mine in the vicinity of Srebrenica. People who live in Srebrenica know very well that the Sasi mine pit is dealing with export. They had also dug a tunnel, a tunnel which reached as far as the outskirts of Srebrenica, and that particular tunnel was used in this military action.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any other vehicles arrive, besides this Lada that you talked about, at any time during the day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: During the day, I didn't, except that Stanimir came in his vehicle. I don't know if it was his or the army's, but it was a red Lada. And then I did not see anything else or, rather, I did not see any other vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In the evenings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, do you think we could make a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. McCloskey, I believe that everybody expects today's session to end at 2.30; however, I see that it was scheduled to last until 3.00. But as you know, we have another Initial Appearance at 3.30, and we need a break for at least some lunch, to have something. So we shall work until 2.30. And that is something that I have to see with the Prosecutor about your schedule for next week. Perhaps at the end of our today's work perhaps you could stop at 2.25. That would be very fine. But now you may continue with your examination of the witness. Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Witness D, did you see any unusual vehicles come that day or that evening to this school area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: As I have said, that Lada was the only vehicle I saw during the day, but sometime in the evening a white Jeep vehicle arrived, and it was driven by the man who had introduced himself as Stanimir earlier in the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell who that white Jeep belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I think that a number of vehicles had been misappropriated from the Dutch Battalion in Srebrenica, and in my view, that vehicle had also been seized from the Dutch Battalion. And later on it was used, as I could see, by Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see any Muslim women or girls get separated and come over to where you were during that day or evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: That evening I noticed only one young woman who had been brought in. She looked rather pretty and quite young, perhaps around 17, and very, very pretty. Serb troops brought her and ordered her to recognise some of us or, rather, to try to identify some of us. And because it was dusk, they used searchlights or headlights. They would focus these lights in our faces so that the girl could perhaps try to identify some of us. But she did not do that, except for one elderly man, and she claimed that he was -- that he lived near her village. Those were villages Tokoljac and Urisici, those two villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what occurred after this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: After that a Serb soldier said, "Well, Turkish girl, aren't you pretty. Go and make us some coffee." And then he made a gesture with his hand towards her face as if to caress her, and she stepped backward, and then he took her by her arm, or rather under her arm, and took her into the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about what time was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It was happening at dusk. Well, it was a summer day and the night begins to fall sometime around 9.00. So I could say that it could have been 9.00, or perhaps slightly after 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And so were all 22 men assembled together with you at that time when she was taken into the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. All 22 men were still in front of the school, together with me, that group of 22. And one of the Serb soldiers approached us and notified us that we would be searched. He said, "You balijas are really difficult to deal with. Perhaps some of you have might have a knife or a pistol or a hand grenade or something like that. We won't run that risk, so we shall search you." As a matter of fact, it turned out that they intended to search us in order to seize money or some valuables, jewellery or rings, things like that. And that appeared to be true when they searched me, and I guess that that is what happened to other men as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell the Court what the meaning of the term "balija" is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that term. I know that some Serb soldiers used it, not all of them. I don't really know what it means. I heard it during the war for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when were you taken in? When was the group taken into the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The group was taken into the school sometime in early evening, or rather when the night had already fallen outside. They said, "You'll be cold outside. You have to go in. There you will be in a classroom." And naturally it was meant cynically. First we entered a classroom, the first one as you enter the building, and then they seemed to change their minds and moved us to the second classroom, next to the first one. What we could see was that the classroom was empty. But let me say first: As we entered the school, as we entered the school building, a Serb soldier had so many pieces of cut wire, that was telephone wire, and they used it to tie our hands behind our backs, all of us. And those of us who had been tied before, they cut it with a knife and then tie them once again with a thin telephone wire, which could be wrapped several times around our wrists and then tied into a knot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what happened after you were taken to the second room, second classroom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: When we entered the second classroom, so we had our hands tied behind our backs, and we were ordered to sit in a corner of that classroom. That was the left corner as you enter the classroom. So it is the left-hand side bottom of the classroom. Men who came in sat down on the floor of that classroom, in that corner. It had a wooden floor, that classroom. I sat somewhere in front of that group. So we were all sitting on the floor. The Serb soldiers left the classroom for a brief moment. Only one Serb soldier remained standing in the doorway, in the entrance to the classroom, sitting on a chair and with an automatic rifle in his lap.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Then I heard the sound of some motor vehicle. I think it was a truck, a lorry, because the sound was quite loud. Immediately after that, a guy appeared in the doorway, I mean, a Serb soldier, and he strode across the floor and said "Who's from (redacted) here?" I immediately recognised him by his voice. That was my friend, my once colleague (redacted). So they had arrived from Kravica and wanted to see which ones of his fellow workers had been brought to the school. When he asked that question -- so he said, "Who's from (redacted) here?" I stood up from where I was sitting and said, "Me, (redacted)." And he recognised me too and said, "What are you doing here?" And I said that I had been wounded in Srebrenica and that I tried to look for rescue in the area of Potocari and that I managed to get there and that I had finally been brought under custody in that school there. Then he said, "I see. Well, this war hasn't been good to you or to us, but what can we do? Right. Very well. See you tomorrow." He just patted me on the shoulder in a friendly manner. As I said, it was quite a friendly gesture. He just patted me on the shoulder and left the school room -- the classroom. Sorry. I can describe what he looked like. (redacted), in comparison, when I had last time seen him, he looked -- he seemed to have some slightly gained in weight than before the war. He had a kerchief tied around his neck, tied behind, and he was wearing a kind of coveralls, a belt, and an automatic rifle in his hands. So he left the classroom, and immediately after that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... for a minute. I'm sorry, but let me ask you a question, if I could. Were you able to notice any rank or any insignia that allowed you to tell what rank he was or what unit he was from, this person you identify as Mr. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: (redacted). No, I did not notice any insignia. Perhaps I forgot to say that there were no lights in the classroom, no electric lights, so that it was lit by a military headlight which was directed at the ceiling, and it was run by the soldiers standing in the doorway. This headlight was turned towards the ceiling, so I really couldn't see any insignia on his uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You were telling us as he left what happened.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. He left, and as soon as he left, perhaps a minute later, Serb troops came in. As soon as they entered or while they were still in the doorway, the Serb guard who was in the doorway talked to them or, rather, he stopped one of those soldiers and wanted to find out how had they fared in Kravica. I heard that question. The question was, "How do you fare in Kravica?" And the other one said, "Oh, great. We've finished with the balijas. We fared great, and we've had no casualties, which is the most important thing." Meanwhile, that group of soldiers, and I think that there were more than ten of them, more than ten of them, so a group of those soldiers came right up to us, and they began to ask questions. Whenever they would ask a question, they would also strike a blow. They started from my left, is, as I was sitting they started from my left dealing blows to people. Whenever they asked a question, and the questions were, for instance, "How many Serbs have you killed? Where is your Naser? Why doesn't he help you? Do you know who are we? Do you know that you'll have to pay for all this?" All sorts of questions like that. And every question was accompanied by a blow. The blow would be with the rifle, on the head. That is, they would hold the rifle in the middle, so they one hit you either with a fist or the rifle on the head, or perhaps kicks in the chest, because people were sitting, so they could kick them easily in any part of the body, and that is how they hit them. They hit an elderly man who was using as a walking stick a metal rod, and that Serb soldier bent down, picked up that metal rod, and continued to beat him with it. I also saw that one of them had a flag, a flag taken of the mosque, that is, a green flag with the central emblem, with the crescent and the star. So he asked those men, "Whose flag is this?" One would say that that was the flag of the mosque, others would say, "I don't know"; the third one, "I don't care." There were all sorts of answers, but whatever the answer, it would be followed with a blow by that metal rod. So when he asked me, I said it was a flag taken off the mosque. And he said, "What mosque? Fuck your balija mother," and I was hit there [indicates], and I will still have quite a visible scar above my right eye, and I began to bleed and blood was coming down my face. Then I was kicked once again on my right so that I tumbled down on my left-hand side and blood, at that point, covered all my face. So I was, therefore, lying on the floor of the classroom. I was not fully conscious by that time but I could still feel. I could still -- I was still aware of what was going on, that is, I had not fainted, but I knew that I wasn't really all there, all present at that moment. This beating lasted for up to half an hour. People were all bloody. I can describe a man who was sitting next to me. He was struck with a knife. At first I thought it was -- he had been struck at the neck, but as he was falling down, I realised that he had been hit in the face and blood spurted down his face. Serb soldiers --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, witness. Excuse me. I understand this was a difficult time for you and the other men, but is it fair to say that this was an awful scene where you were beaten and your group was beaten by these soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had you seen this group of ten soldiers before during the day or was this the first time that they'd showed up at the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No. They did not appear as I described it when I described Mr. (redacted) uniform. They were wearing the same kind of uniform. It was a coverall uniform, and the Serb soldiers during the daytime did not have that kind of uniforms, nor did they wear any bandannas, and those Serb soldiers, all those guys had bandannas of different colours. Some were tied in the back such as their special units, rather, sabotage units wore it. They had it. That was part of their image.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you tell from their accents where they were from, this group of soldiers that did the beating?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Judging by their speech, it was quite normal. They spoke like all the other people who lived in Srebrenica and around it. That is, it was quite a normal speech, and I cannot really say if they came from somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What happened after they finished beating all you people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I should say first that a Serb soldier, that is, one of their comrades came, "It's time," and when he said, "It's time," the other one asked him what time was it, and he said it was 12.00 or, rather, 2400, 2400. So that was the 13th. Immediately after that, a minute or two later, they left the classroom, and I decided that they had to go somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Had you, at this time, seen or heard from the woman that was taken in the classroom? Excuse me, taken into the school.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Before this group entered, I could hear this young woman's screams, and I think that he started to run across the passage. What was she crying out? "Let me go. Don't touch me," or something like that. But that stopped abruptly, and after that I did not hear a single sound come from that young woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. What happened after the soldiers that did the beating left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: When those soldiers who beat us left the classroom, several, I think some five or six soldiers, entered, those who were next to the school during the daytime. One of them turned to us and said, "Don't say that they beat you," and it was said with a great deal of cynicism. I mean, the soldier could see people were bleeding all over. Then he said, "Right. Now you'll stand up and stand against the wall." And he said it in a normal voice, but because nobody could stand up or nobody did stand up, then he shouted, then he yelled it at us. And when I saw that several men from this group had managed to stand up by the wall, then I tried to do the same, because I was afraid I would be beaten once again. So I complied with the order, and I stood against the wall. Those men could not -- simply could not manage to stand for long. They just simply slid down the wall, I suppose because they had been beaten so badly. So they simply couldn't stand. Their feet wouldn't hold them. The same happened to me. So we were back on the floor once again. He saw what the situation was. He realised that men had been severely beaten, and then he said, "Right. Now you'll go to repair our outhouses," but I thought that he said we had to go repair their trenches. That is what I thought he had said. He said, "You'll come out of the classroom one by one. There is a truck waiting for you. You will get onto the truck and everything will be fine." So in front of me was one man. Then I came. And as soon as I came out of the school, I saw the truck which was parked right next to the stairs that I mentioned. And the truck came to the -- it came to those stairs with its back to the stairs, and the ramp was adjusted so it fitted the stairs. And a Serb soldier who was at the bottom of the truck said, contrary to what the previous soldier said, that we are going to repair trenches, he said that we were to go to a military prison and that it would be quite nice there. And he said, "Don't be afraid. Everything will be all right. So sit on the right-hand bench and leave the left-hand bench free." So this man who was walking in front of me was the first one who sat on the right-hand bench, next to the cabin of the truck; and then I was the next one; and then other men -- I don't know how many men -- sat down on that bench. Those people who could not climb the truck by themselves, the Serb soldiers, two Serb soldiers, would simply pick them up and bring them on and simply loaded them onto that truck. They were just loaded one over the other, heaped together, lying on their backs or on their side, or perhaps they moved only slightly. They were all lying there. And they checked the number after they had loaded all of them. They simply counted everybody and established that there were 22 men in that truck. The left-hand bench was still quite empty and I tried to think why was that so, and then realised that -- then I saw that four Serb soldiers took that left bench. And three Serb soldiers went into the cabin of the truck, the driver and the other two, and the truck set off. On the first map which we saw, I said that I would tell you about that road later. So we took that path behind the school, got to the road, and turned to Vlasenica. It was moving rather fast and that air was quite refreshing, so that I felt slightly better. But I have to describe the truck now. It was a conventional military truck with military benches, and I know that, because I had served the Yugoslav People's Army. And it has no tarpaulin, but it has some -- it has the skeleton for the tarpaulin, but there was no tarpaulin. And so the truck went on towards Vlasenica, and the Serb soldiers who were in the truck said, "Don't you even think of fleeing, because you could get killed, as we shall then have to open fire on you."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness D. Can I interrupt you for a minute? Can you tell us, the soldiers who got in the truck, both in the cabin and the back, were those soldiers familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Those in the truck, no. One Serb soldier who boarded the cabin during the previous day, he had introduced himself as the commander of these men next to the school, and allegedly he had also suffered as a prisoner of the BH Army. And he said, "Well, that is the least what you can expect too." That is what I remembered about that Serb soldier, and I remember him, and he boarded the cabin of the truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So did the truck drive on towards Vlasenica and eventually turn off to the left of the road before going into the town of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. They ordered us to look -- to keep our eyes on the floor, not to look around, and the only thing I could see were the lights of a town; that is, rather, I felt that suddenly we found ourselves in a lit street. So we were already at the entry into Vlasenica when the bus turned left and took a macadam road. And as we were riding, I kept thinking about how to try to jump off the truck, but I realised that that would be a very ugly leap which could also mean death. And I couldn't jump anyway, because my hands were tied at the back. But as I was leaning --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you again. Sorry. Did you hear the soldiers on the truck communicate with each other about anything at some point on this drive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: At some point, when the truck turned left, it reached a small stream, a brook, which was overgrown with ferns and other grass, and I couldn't really see anything there. But it stopped there briefly, and a Serb soldier who was in that truck, with his fist, knocked on the roof of the cabin, that is, above the driver, and said, "Not here. Take them up there, where they took people before." He said it very loudly and it was quite clear. The driver understood him, so that the truck proceeded. And I have to explain here that I was trying to somehow undo the knot on the wire that was around my wrists. So on that bar there was a metal part, and I suppose it must have been a screw of the tarpaulin frame. And as I leaned backward, I could simply feel that screw, how it pricked me. And I was trying to use that screw somehow to undo the knot around my wrists. I did not manage to do that, but I loosened the knot, because this telephone wire is quite flexible. I don't know whether you know that that wire can even be torn apart, because it is only a single-thread wire. However, in my case there may have been several threads in that wire, but I nevertheless managed to loosen it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did shortly after that the truck reach its destination and then stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you briefly describe the area that the truck stopped in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There is a great deal that I learned later on. As we were making our way through, I learned from a man who was in our group, whom I had told that I had escaped the execution, and I described him the way I took. So he explained to me exactly where it was that we were taken. This man, who was explaining this to me, was from the area, from the environs of Cerska, so he knew quite well the region and he was sure about the place he indicated, and he told me it was Rasica Gaj. So it's a small place, not far from Vlasenica, on the left side of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We don't need to know exactly where it was, but can you just describe: Was it dark out, light out? What kind of an area was it that the truck stopped in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I can do that. The truck stopped in an elevation after it had moved uphill, and there was a little clearing or a pasture there that was probably abandoned and was an overgrown meadow. I saw a partly demolished house there. It was rather a not-finished house; it had only one floor and the rest of the house had collapsed. So the truck stopped near that house. The engine was turned off but the lights, the headlights, remained lit. So those soldiers, the ones who were on the truck, got off the truck -- there were four of them -- and I was sitting in the left corner of the truck. They opened the front part of the truck and three other soldiers got out of the cabin, the ones who had been there, and they stayed near the truck, opposite from the place where I was sitting. So I was facing them at that time. The three of them were there. And one of the group, which consisted of four Serb soldiers, approached the ones that had been in the cabin. He probably needed to talk to them about something. The three men immediately set out on their job. They started killing people. The killing started by shooting down the people who were standing -- who were actually piled up on the bottom of the truck. I think most of them had been badly beaten up. One of them may have even been already dead. So they were quite weak. They would simply throw them off the truck and then, with short bursts of gunfire, finish them off. The second and the third man experienced the same fate, but two other men who were sitting on the bench next to me tried to escape. They jumped off the truck and they manage to cover some 20 meters in the rear from the truck. I was able to observe all this. It was very clear to me what was happening. The Serb soldiers who were standing next to the rear of the truck opened fire on them and they were hit. One of them fell on his chest; the other one fell on his side. The one who fell on his side shivered a little bit as he was passing away. At that moment I managed to free one of my hands and I -- as soon as I had done that, I leaned -- or rather, I grabbed one side of the truck, the one that was on my back, and I jumped off the truck. This was immediately noticed by one of the persons standing next to the cabin of the truck, and he shouted, "Look at this balija motherfucker. He's fleeing, he's escaping." So they immediately opened fire from all of their weapons. There was lots of gunfire at that moment, but I could feel the bullets hit the shrubbery which was a little above me. I could hear this siffling sound and I could hear bullets falling all around me and I realised that I had to stay on the ground. What was working to my advantage was the fact that they had to shoot above the truck because of where they were standing. The truck was actually between us. So both groups had to shoot over the truck. It was nighttime. If you have followed my story, we were still in school at midnight, so it must have been sometime after midnight. I was also assisted by the fact that the forest was nearby. I managed to get to the forest, and I was at that time hit by a branch. I couldn't see anything in the forest; it was pitch dark. And I fell down on the ground and I rolled down a slope. It was a very steep and long slope, and I managed to reach the bottom rather quickly. I could still hear bursts of gunfire. Some of it was coming from the vicinity, some of it from a distance, and I concluded that the gunfire coming from the vicinity was from the group who was following me and that the other gunfire was opened near the truck. So I reached a brook, where I stayed for a while. I couldn't continue. I couldn't see anything; it was dark. And I remained hidden behind a rock, as a kind of shelter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did you feel then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: It was very difficult for me at the time. I think it was the worst moment and the most difficult moment of my life. Or perhaps not the most difficult one. The most difficult one was when my child was taken away from me, and because of the fact that I couldn't utter a single word to my child as she was being taken away. But this time I felt that I was free, but I also thought that they would find me and that their threats would become true. I thought that there was no way for me to escape, that I would be captured again, that I would be tortured again, and I thought about this possibility of being tortured intensely and I was afraid. My whole body was shivering. I was trembling, as if in a great cold, as if I were freezing. So this lasted for a while, this situation I had found myself in, probably throughout the night, until the dawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it true that for the next approximately seven days you wandered around the area trying to find the free territory by yourself, living off the land?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. I spent seven days wandering around. I had no food whatsoever. I lived on what I could find on the land -- a mushroom here and there, some apples, plums -- and I was very weak as a result of that. I still had my injury. My leg had been injured and the wound became infected, so this was an additional problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is it true that for another approximately seven days after that you were able to meet up with other Muslim men in a similar situation, and finally on the last day you and a few others were able to escape to the asphalt road near Kladanj? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. A little more than seven days, I think. On the 27th of July, to be more precise, I managed to reach the free territory, and I ran into a group of people with whom I then continued along the brook, along a small river, which was actually situated on no man's land, between two lines. The area was mined, and we saw a lot of bodies along the brook. I think we saw more than a dozen of corpses in the brook which was called Jezernica. It probably got its name because of small waterfalls. It was not an easily accessible brook, and the whole area was not easily accessible, but it was still mined. So I was in a group of those people. One of them stepped on a mine, and as a result of that four people were injured. I could only hear them scream. I glanced in their direction and I saw that two bodies were bleeding heavily. I didn't notice anybody else, but I presume that four people were immediately injured after that explosion. What followed was gunfire by some Serbian soldiers who were there lying in an ambush. It was terrible. There was a lot of gunfire from light weapons, from hand-held rocket launchers, rifles, and so on and so forth. But we were assisted by a number of large boulders, large rocks, so we managed to step from one to another, hiding between those rocks. I was again wounded on that occasion, but my wounds were not as serious as the wounds of other people in the group. The four of us who were not injured in the mining incident were again wounded in the gunfire. One of us was severely wounded, but the three of us managed to reach the asphalt road. But once we were there, we were completely disoriented; we didn't know which way to go. Since I was in the best condition, I decided which way we should go. We continued for another five or six hundred meters, and at that point we ran into two white vehicles. The first vehicle stopped, came near us, and the driver spoke to us. He was speaking, he was addressing us in a foreign language. I believe he was speaking English, but we couldn't understand him. There was another vehicle following the first one, and this other driver spoke Bosnian. And he said, "I can see you have been wounded. Do you need any help?" So one of us couldn't trust that person, but the person then showed us his identification card, some kind of card, at least, and we believed him. So we entered the vehicles, and shortly after that we found ourselves in the free territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names of the people you knew that died that night outside that truck?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There were few people whom I knew. Those were Rizo, who was a neighbour of mine, and he used to work for the Dutch Battalion as an electrician. I don't remember his family name. Then there was a Fuad; two brothers from the village of Bajramovici, near Srebrenica; Azem Becic, the man from the village of Kotjevac. He was wounded. He was walking with crutches. Then there was a man called Sajko, from the village of Jagodnja; Abdul Kadir, another paramedic. There were actually two paramedics. One of them was Hasan, who used to work in the hospital, during peacetime, in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And many others that you do not know.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, and many others whose names I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Petrusic or Mr. Visnjic, how long do you expect the cross-examination to take, if you are in a position to tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course Mr. President. I assume that it will take much longer than the time that has remained today for us, but I should like to take this opportunity to raise a question of principle which is closely related to this situation.
